title: choose the argument *before the campaign*
dek: A focused decision room for what The Angle Map should lead with, how it should be tested, and what the current evidence does not yet prove.
lens: message decision · proof boundary · market test
sources: current offer record · founding intake · proof counters

sections.heading: the decision
sections.body:
The Angle Map should lead with one idea: choose the campaign argument before funding more creative around it.

That is the clearest expression of the service's value. It positions the work as a decision product, not an option generator. The evidence-safe and 48-hour dimensions strengthen the promise, but neither should replace the main argument.

rows.evidence: One live message read, three campaign angles, approved-proof direction, claim-safety boundaries, and one lead recommendation are delivered for one occasion.

rows.claim: The service is a decision product
rows.evidence: Its deliverable settles which campaign argument to build first and what evidence may support it; it does not promise execution performance.

rows.claim: The proposed buyer problem is testable but not yet qualified
rows.evidence: The current evidence does not include direct customer interviews, purchases, or exposure results connecting the problem to the proposed segment.

items.action: 1 · Decide before you fund more creative
items.why: Lead belief: weak campaigns often begin with an unresolved argument, not a shortage of creative options. Best use: offer introduction and decision-note test.

items.action: 2 · Make the proof choose the message
items.why: Supporting belief: usable evidence and claim boundaries should shape the direction before copy expands. Best use: proof-sensitive buyers and regulated categories.

items.action: 3 · Settle the campaign argument in 48 hours
items.why: Supporting belief: a bounded decision can move quickly without becoming careless. Best use: deadline-driven occasions after scope and source readiness are confirmed.
It names the strategic mistake the service is designed to avoid and makes the decision product easier to understand.

items.action: Use Angle 2 as the proof mechanism
items.why: It shows why the recommendation is disciplined without implying legal or regulatory approval.

items.action: Use Angle 3 as the delivery feature
items.why: Speed reduces delay, but it should not carry the positioning by itself.

items.action: Do not blend all three into one headline
items.why: One message should organize the test; the other two should answer why the work is credible and timely.

blocks.label: MESSAGE SHELL
blocks.text: Your next campaign creates one decision before more creative gets built: which buyer belief and approved proof should organize the work first. I mapped the available evidence into a one-page Decision Note showing the tradeoff, the proof question, and what I would not force into the same campaign. Would that decision note be useful?

blocks.label: FIRST BATCH
blocks.text: Five qualified recipients. Keep the segment, problem, useful object, and message fixed. No messages should be sent until the batch and recipients are separately approved.

blocks.label: WHAT COUNTS
blocks.text: Count meaningful response, direct problem confirmation, Decision Note request, held conversation, unchanged $750 acceptance, and cleared payment separately.

blocks.label: DECISION RULE
blocks.text: Continue when at least 2 of 5 respond meaningfully and at least 1 confirms the problem. Repair only the failed gate when qualification, value, or language misses. Retire the segment/problem hypothesis after 10 qualified exposures plus an approved follow-up produce zero problem confirmations.

sections.heading: evidence boundary
sections.kicker: WHAT THIS ROOM DOES NOT CLAIM
sections.body: This room confirms a clear service scope and a disciplined message hypothesis. It does not prove that the proposed segment experiences the problem, that the message will convert, or that buyers will pay. The three angles remain candidates until real customer language and market behavior exist. The work maps editorial direction to approved evidence; legal and compliance approval remain with the client's qualified reviewer.
